newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FEATURE - Sweden's moose hunters hit by weather, disease.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Sweden's moose hunters hit by weather, disease.

text.p: Unusually warm weather and a mysterious wasting disease have hampered the start of Sweden's annual moose shooting season.

Every year hunters in Sweden kill more moose than any other country in the world, shooting an estimated 19,000 of the large, lumbering forest dwellers during the three-month season which starts in September.

Apart from North America, Scandinavia is the only region in which this imposing ungulate can be hunted on any significant scale and every year hundreds of people travel to Sweden to join hunting parties on the moose trail.
But the season, which started in northern Sweden on September 2 and spreads down the country over the next month, has had a disappointing start -- from the hunter's point of view.

As well as battling seasonal difficulties, this year hunters are facing stricter limitations on the number of moose they can set their sights on, with the country's moose population on the decline, now estimated at around 300,000.

"We had an explosion in the moose population about 10 years ago but numbers are now falling again so we have to restrict shooting numbers this year," Hakan Collin, head of a shooting association in central Sweden told Reuters.
"Local councils set the limits but most regions across the country are only allowing shooters to take out 20 moose for every 4,000 hectares (9,880 acres) compared to 40 in 1985."
A mysterious wasting disease that first appeared in Sweden in 1985 has had a small impact on moose numbers so far and left scientists baffled over its cause and origin.

Veterinary surgeon Margareta Steen from Sweden's agricultural university in Uppsala said at least 1,400 of the animals, a species of moose also called the European elk, have died so far from the disease that is characterised by abnormal behaviour, blindness, and wasting.
"It has been worse so far in the south of Sweden but we are getting more reports from all over the country and even from Norway, from areas that border Sweden," Steen told Reuters.
"We have had 1,400 deaths recorded but we have no idea how many animals have really died from this disease or how quickly it is spreading."
But Bjorn Gunarfelt, a licencing official from Lulea in the far north of Sweden, said the unusually warm summer had had the most impact on the new season.

"The problem is that when you shoot a moose and gut it you need to be able to hang the body up somewhere cold, in a temperature of four to five degrees Celsius (41 degrees Fahrenheit)," Gunarfelt told Reuters.
"It has been too hot this season. We have had temperatures of between 10 to 15 degrees Celsius (50- 59 degrees Fahrenheit) and in this weather you get too many mosquitoes that lay eggs in the meat."
The moose is Sweden's largest mammal and a popular symbol of its forest wilderness -- and on the nation's dining tables.

Collin said the animals were a pest to drivers who fared badly if they hit one of the long-legged animals that can stand 235 cm (nearly eight feet) tall and weigh between 500 and 700 kg (1,100 and 1,540 lbs).
Moose warning signs, a yellow triangle with a dark silhouette outline of a loping moose, are common along country roads, warning drivers to be on the look-out.
Collin said as well as posing a hazard to motorists, moose also caused extensive damage to Sweden's forests so numbers had to be kept under control.
Even though the majority of Swedes are in favour of the moose shooting season, there is still a national affection for the slow-witted beast.

Souvenir shops lining Stockholm's busiest thoroughfare, Drottningsgatan, offer a vast range of moose souvenirs ranging from wooden moose massagers -- apparently very popular with pregnant women -- to fridge magnets, cuddly toys, carpets, and glasses.
Earrings made from moose droppings glazed with 10 layers of varnish came onto the market a few years ago but failed to attract too many wearers.
Sweden's first moose farm has just opened at Bjurholm where the owners plan to make moose cheese, milk and yoghurt.
"Everyone loves moose but the reasons for the shooting season are logical so there are no objections," said Collin.
"They are very good to eat but you can also use the skin for leather, getting about 100 to 150 crowns ($15-20) a skin."
